Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

Content:
[MATH: 0^{∘} ≤ x < 360^{∘}.]

Content:
We can immediately calculate a solution, called the principal value, as follows:
[MATH: x = \arctan\left(\sqrt{3}\right) = 60^\circ]

Content:
Since [MATH: 60^\circ] lies inside the required domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1=60^\circ.]

Content:
The tangent function has a period of [MATH: 180^\circ.] So, to generate more solutions, we add (or subtract) integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] to the principal value.

Content:
Therefore, our second solution [MATH: x_2] inside the range [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ] can be calculated as

Content:
[MATH: x_{2}|= x_{1} + 180^{∘}; = 60^{∘} + 180^{∘}; = 240^{∘}.]

Content:
We can stop generating solutions here because adding or subtracting further integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] to the principal value will give us solutions that lie outside the domain [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
So, the solutions are [MATH: x=60^\circ, 240^\circ.]

sections.normalized_html: Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 3\tan x + 3\sqrt{3}=0] for [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]
sections.readable_text: Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 3\tan x + 3\sqrt{3}=0] for [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we rearrange the equation and isolate [MATH: \tan x \mathbin{:}] [MATH: 3\tan x + 3sqrt(3)|= 0; 3\tan x|= − 3sqrt(3); \tan x|= − (3sqrt(3))/(3); \tan x|= − sqrt(3).] Next, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arctan (− sqrt(3)) = − 60^{∘}]

Since [MATH: -60^\circ] lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution. However, to generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] as follows: [MATH: x_{1}|= x + 180^{∘} = − 60^{∘} + 180^{∘} = 120^{∘}] [MATH: x_{2}|= x + 360^{∘} = − 60^{∘} + 360^{∘} = 300^{∘}]

So, the solutions are [MATH: x=120^\circ, 300^\circ.]

Explanation:

[MATH: 3\tan x + 3sqrt(3)|= 0; 3\tan x|= − 3sqrt(3); \tan x|= − (3sqrt(3))/(3); \tan x|= − sqrt(3).]

[MATH: x = \arctan (− sqrt(3)) = − 60^{∘}]

So, the solutions (rounded to the nearest integer) are [MATH: x=76^\circ, 256^\circ.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

Content:
[MATH: 0^{∘} ≤ x < 360^{∘}.]

Content:
We can immediately calculate a solution, called the principal value, as follows:
[MATH: x = \arctan\left(\sqrt{3}\right) = 60^\circ]

Content:
Since [MATH: 60^\circ] lies inside the required domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1=60^\circ.]

Content:
The tangent function has a period of [MATH: 180^\circ.] So, to generate more solutions, we add (or subtract) integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] to the principal value.

Content:
Therefore, our second solution [MATH: x_2] inside the range [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ] can be calculated as

Content:
[MATH: x_{2}|= x_{1} + 180^{∘}; = 60^{∘} + 180^{∘}; = 240^{∘}.]

Content:
We can stop generating solutions here because adding or subtracting further integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] to the principal value will give us solutions that lie outside the domain [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
So, the solutions are [MATH: x=60^\circ, 240^\circ.]

Item 2 — Example: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Tangent with Special Angles

Example Prompt:
Find the solutions to the equation [MATH: 3\tan x + 3\sqrt{3}=0] for [MATH: 0^\circ \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we rearrange the equation and isolate [MATH: \tan x \mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 3\tan x + 3sqrt(3)|= 0; 3\tan x|= − 3sqrt(3); \tan x|= − (3sqrt(3))/(3); \tan x|= − sqrt(3).]
Next, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arctan (− sqrt(3)) = − 60^{∘}]

Since [MATH: -60^\circ] lies outside the given domain, it is not a solution. However, to generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] as follows:
[MATH: x_{1}|= x + 180^{∘} = − 60^{∘} + 180^{∘} = 120^{∘}]
[MATH: x_{2}|= x + 360^{∘} = − 60^{∘} + 360^{∘} = 300^{∘}]

So, the solutions are [MATH: x=120^\circ, 300^\circ.]

Item 5 — Example: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Tangent with Non-Special Angles

Example Prompt:
Calculate, in degrees to the nearest integer, the solutions to the equation [MATH: \tan x=4] for [MATH: 0 \leq x < 360^\circ.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arctan (4) = 75.96375...^{∘} ≈ 75.964^{∘}]

Since [MATH: 75.964^\circ] lies inside the given domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 = 75.964^\circ.]

To generate more solutions, we add integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] as follows:

[MATH: x_2 = 180^\circ + 75.964^\circ \approx 255.964^\circ]

So, the solutions (rounded to the nearest integer) are [MATH: x=76^\circ, 256^\circ.]

Item 8 — Tutorial: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Tangent Under a Modified Domain

Content:
Suppose we want to find all of the solutions to the equation

Content:
[MATH: − 180^{∘} < x ≤ 180^{∘}.]

Content:
Notice that this time, we are looking for solutions in the domain [MATH: -180^\circ < x \leq 180^\circ.]

Content:
First, we find the principal value:
[MATH: x = \arctan (1) = 45^{∘}]

Content:
Since [MATH: 45^\circ] lies inside the given domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 =45^\circ.]

Content:
To generate more solutions, we subtract integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ,] as follows:

Content:
[MATH: x_{2}|= x_{1} − 180^{∘}; = 45^{∘} − 180^{∘}; = − 135^{∘}]

Content:
So, the solutions are [MATH: x=-135^\circ, 45^\circ.]

Item 9 — Example: Solving a Trigonometric Equation Involving Tangent Under a Modified Domain

Example Prompt:
Solve the equation [MATH: 3 \tan x - \sqrt{3} = 0] for [MATH: -180^\circ < x \leq 180^\circ.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we rearrange the equation, isolating [MATH: \tan x \mathbin{:}]
[MATH: 3\tan x − sqrt(3)|= 0; 3\tan x|= sqrt(3); \tan x|= (sqrt(3))/(3)]

Now, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arctan ((sqrt(3))/(3)) = 30^{∘}]

Since [MATH: 30^\circ] lies inside the given domain, our first solution is [MATH: x_1 =30^\circ.]

To generate more solutions, we subtract integer multiples of [MATH: 180^\circ] as follows:

[MATH: x_{2}|= x_{1} − 180^{∘}; = 30^{∘} − 180^{∘}; = − 150^{∘}]

So, the solutions are [MATH: x=-150^\circ, 30^\circ.]

Item 12 — Example: Finding the Points of Intersection of a Horizontal Line and a Tangent Curve

Example Prompt:
The graph below shows a section of the curve [MATH: y=\tan{x}] on the interval [MATH: -\dfrac \pi 2 < x < \dfrac {\pi} 2] and the line [MATH: y=1.] The line and the curve intersect at the point [MATH: A,] as shown. What is the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the point [MATH: A?]

[IMG: /graphics/75d3912698b1187b3fc86e2e9db62892]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
The [MATH: y]-values of both functions are the same at the intersection point. Equating the two functions gives

[MATH: \tan x=1, \qquad -\dfrac \pi 2 < x < \dfrac {\pi} 2 .]

First, we find the principal value:

[MATH: x = \arctan (1) = (π)/(4)]

Since [MATH: \dfrac{\pi}{4}] lies inside the required domain, and there is only one point of intersection, we conclude that the [MATH: x]-coordinate of the intersection point [MATH: A] is [MATH: x= \dfrac{\pi}{4}.]
